scope: Mexican sonidero and adjacent regional routes; research and integration gate, not a claim that all entries share one rhythm.

rules.newPreset: Requires a source-labelled rhythm cell or a named practitioner-approved role map, an explicit statement of what has been authored, and a distinct display name.
rules.performanceControl: May be implemented from mechanism evidence, but must not be relabelled as a regional canonical accompaniment.
rules.repertoireFamily: Requires its own source chain; a repertoire listing alone cannot become a step grid.
rules.compoundMeter: Do not flatten a documented 6/8 or 12/8 practice into the current 2/4 or 4/4 engine. It remains a product-engine requirement until compound meter is supported.

cdmx-decree-2023.claim: The declaration describes Cultura Sonidera as a social/performance practice and lists cumbia, salsa, guaracha, vallenato, chicha and son montuno among the repertoires circulated at public dances.
cdmx-decree-2023.doesNotEstablish: A universal drum grid, an exclusive city ownership of a genre, or a transcription right.

puebla-cuetlaxcoapan-2023.claim: The article documents cumbia sonidera as a lived Puebla practice across neighbourhood, peripheral and public-event contexts.
puebla-cuetlaxcoapan-2023.doesNotEstablish: One Poblano accompaniment pattern or a device-specific production method.

puebla-local-listening-categories.claim: The Puebla dossier records local listener categories: slow lyrical poblanas, fast constant-tempo Peruvian/Andean material, and peñoneras whose recurring changes of rhythm and speed support more elaborate dancing.
puebla-local-listening-categories.doesNotEstablish: A fixed instrumentation, a canonical 16-step pattern for any category, that Peruvian repertory is Mexican, or permission to use the category names as unqualified product genres.

lippman-2018.claim: Fieldwork supports treating selection, voice, dedications and mixer intervention as live sonidero practice.
lippman-2018.doesNotEstablish: A fixed genre tempo or a stock spoken sample.

felini-regional-roles.claim: Ima Felini distinguishes the CDMX sonidera instrumentation from a more synthesizer-forward Poblana vocabulary and treats wepa as a separate approach.
felini-regional-roles.doesNotEstablish: A complete regional grid, a universal local instrumentation, or an attribution for any individual programmed note.

colmex-wepa.claim: A Colegio de México study records the Potosí use of wepa as a music/sound-world associated with deep voices announcing names, barrios and greetings over a cumbia-like rhythm; it distinguishes the term from sonidero itself.
colmex-wepa.doesNotEstablish: One drum pattern, a complete Wepa instrumentation, a pre-recorded vocal device, or a claim that the current Compás study reproduces Kiss Sound.

monterrey-rebajada.claim: Monterrey rebajada scholarship supports a distinct local record/playback history.

ucsbc-rebajada.claim: The archive describes Sonido Dueñez's experimental tape-based rebajada practice in working-class Monterrey.
ucsbc-rebajada.doesNotEstablish: That slowed playback belongs solely to Monterrey or maps to one loop.

rock-sonidero.claim: The programme identifies a Neza/Chimalhuacán rock-sonidero history and notes a need for more systematic research.

mixteca-tecladistas.claim: INAH fieldwork documents Mixteca Baja tecladistas carrying local instrumentation and repertoire forward; it describes cumbia influence in the bass, sonidero greetings, and yaa sii/chilena in 6/8 or 12/8 with distinct fast and slow variants.
mixteca-tecladistas.doesNotEstablish: That yaa sii is cumbia, that its compound meter can be faithfully reduced to Compás's current straight-meter engine, or a stock sound/step grid.

inah-yaa-sii-12-8.claim: An INAH publication identifies the dactylic tetragroup in yaa sii as equivalent to 12/8 and distinguishes Mixtec yaa sii from the coastal chilena label used in Spanish translation.
inah-yaa-sii-12-8.doesNotEstablish: A universal kick/conga grid, a device arrangement, or that a 12/8 pattern can replace local melody, language, instrumentation or performance practice.

ecmo-chilena-meter-2025.claim: The ECMO account characterises chilena practice through dactylic rhythms in 6/8 or 12/8 and notes sesquialtera more strongly toward the coast.
ecmo-chilena-meter-2025.doesNotEstablish: That Mixteca Baja yaa sii and coastal chilena are interchangeable, or an exact accompaniment reduction for Compás.

cumbia-sureste-lead.claim: A regional overview distinguishes cumbia del sureste from Oaxaca/Guerrero sureña, CDMX tropical and northern cumbia, and describes a sax, keyboard, drum and tumbadora-oriented ensemble route.
cumbia-sureste-lead.doesNotEstablish: A primary-source transcription, a stable name accepted in every locality, or an exact pattern suitable for release.

unicach-chunchaca.claim: The thesis distinguishes cumbia del sureste/Chunchaca as a Mexican regional route and describes acoustic kit, tumbadoras, horn space, occasional synth/electric-guitar colour and a flexible bass practice in ensemble performance.
unicach-chunchaca.doesNotEstablish: A fixed 16-step loop, a universal tempo, a specific recording's bass line, or an interchangeable label for every southeastern musician.

enes-sureste-2026.claim: ENES Mérida traces cumbia's local adaptation in the southeast and identifies sax/metals, bass, güiro and drum kit as part of the regional ensemble colour.
enes-sureste-2026.doesNotEstablish: An exact rhythm transcription or a single style for the whole region.

inah-central-sonidero-circuit.claim: INAH describes a sonidero practice that grew from Mexico City into Estado de México, Morelos, Puebla, Tlaxcala and Hidalgo, and identifies Puebla, Tlaxcala, Hidalgo and Morelos as states with active sonidero communities.
inah-central-sonidero-circuit.doesNotEstablish: A different drum grammar for every state, a fixed circuit repertoire, or a right to call one preset definitive for the corridor.

unam-tropical-repertoire.claim: A UNAM study describes light-and-sound events as a tropical repertoire practice built around cumbia and salsa while also circulating sones, porros, vallenatos, guarachas, charangas, rumba and other Latin American forms; it distinguishes repertoire selection from one uniform rhythm.
unam-tropical-repertoire.doesNotEstablish: That each repertory name is a local Mexican subgenre, a complete step grid, or a performance right in a copied recording.

radio-educacion-digital-charanga.claim: Radio Educación describes Digital Charanga as a cumbia-sonidera project that combines pre-recorded digital tracks with live musicians and is designed for dancing.
radio-educacion-digital-charanga.doesNotEstablish: That the project represents every sonidero, a transferable rhythm pattern, or a right to copy its arrangements.

leon-cumbia-editada-lead.claim: A scene report identifies computer-made cumbia editada layered over older songs in León as a local practice worth investigating.
leon-cumbia-editada-lead.doesNotEstablish: A primary-source history, a stable genre definition, a canonical beat, or an implementation-ready pattern.

lanes.claim: An authored accompaniment with room for live speech and record-style selection.
lanes.nextGate: Named-record rhythm cell or practitioner-reviewed role map.

lanes.claim: An authored keyboard-and-timbal study; not a stand-in for all Puebla practice.
lanes.nextGate: Puebla musician comparison of instrumental roles and dance phrase.

lanes.claim: Poblana, Peruvian/Andean and peñonera are locally reported listening and dance categories; they guide arrangement behaviour but are not yet three eligible Compás rhythm identities.
lanes.nextGate: For a source-cell arrangement, identify the relevant repertoire and its named source; for a performance feature, prototype a player-controlled phrase/tempo transition and obtain Puebla dancer-musician review.

lanes.claim: An authored cumbia/dub crossover study, deliberately distinct from rebajada.
A rate-and-pitch playback transform, not a preset rhythm.
lanes.nextGate: Preserve coupled pitch, speed and tails; no new beat name.

lanes.claim: An authored Potosí Wepa-context accompaniment, held separate from Puebla and tribal; its programmed cuts are Compás choices, while the documented deep-voice/saludo layer remains live and unprogrammed.
lanes.nextGate: Potosí operator and musician review of rhythmic roles, pace and a player-authored live saludo route.

lanes.claim: A separate Compás club study; never rendered as a sonidero sub-beat.
Named repertoire families in sonidero programming, each requiring its own rhythm evidence.
lanes.nextGate: Use only their individual source-cell ledgers.

lanes.claim: Repertoire families in the documented programming ecology.
lanes.nextGate: Document local route, named source and player roles before a Compás lane.

lanes.claim: A named local history requiring a source dossier before any musical reduction.
lanes.nextGate: Oral-history and source discovery; no pattern implementation.

lanes.claim: A public label retained as an unresolved research lead.
lanes.nextGate: Named performer/record, geography and role map.

lanes.claim: A keyboard-led Mixteca Baja practice with its own local identity; cumbia influence and sonidero greetings are documented, but it is not a cumbia-sonidera preset.
lanes.nextGate: Compound-meter editor/target qualification, then a Mixteca practitioner-approved role map and language-aware presentation. The 12/8 evidence supports a timing model, not a named factory loop.

lanes.claim: An authored Compás accompaniment using documented ensemble roles, kept separate from Mexican cumbia sureña and CDMX sonidera.
lanes.nextGate: Southeast musician review of balance, tempo range and the decision to leave the lead line unprogrammed.

lanes.claim: A connected central-Mexican circuit of sonidero communities, not evidence that CDMX, Estado de México, Morelos, Puebla, Tlaxcala and Hidalgo each require an invented proprietary beat.
lanes.nextGate: Collect participant-led role maps or named-record cells from a particular locality before adding a geographically named rhythm; until then, improve set, saludo and cue workflows rather than multiplying presets.

lanes.claim: Sonidero programming is a repertoire-routing practice across distinct tropical forms, rather than a cumbia-only genre menu.
lanes.nextGate: Add only individually sourced cells for a named family; a set browser may group them as repertoire without claiming rhythmic equivalence.

lanes.claim: A documented cumbia-sonidera project combines digital backing with musicians playing live, supporting a one-man-band design that leaves lead and response roles available to the performer.
lanes.nextGate: Interview practitioners before naming a rhythm lane; prototype an accompaniment mode with intentional open lead space rather than a canned band imitation.

lanes.claim: Computer-edited cumbia is a credible local production lead, but the current evidence is a scene report rather than a source chain sufficient for a Compás study.
lanes.nextGate: Find a practitioner account plus a named, licensable/analysable work or player-approved role map; do not add an EDITADA beat from the present lead.
